(3) And look! They saw stars in the East. And they (the stars) led them (the magi) until they came to the cave, and it (the star) stood over the head of the child. And when the magi saw him with his mother Mary, they took gifts from their bags: gold, and frankincense, and myrrh. And having been warned by the angel, they returned to their country by another way. Notes Chapter 5: the plate worn by the priest. Literally, “the leaf of the priest.” Possibly a reference to the metal disk worn on the priest’s forehead, as described in Exodus 28:36-38 and 39:30, 31. Cf. Ronald F. Hock, The Infancy Gospels of James and Thomas (Polebridge Press), 1995, p. 39. Chapter 8: pollute the sanctuary. I.e., by menstruation. Chapter 10: On the elite group of young women responsible for spinning the Temple veil, cf. Cf. Megan Nutzman, “Mary in the Protoevangelium of James: A Jewish Woman in the Temple?” Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies (2013), Vol. 53, pp. 563-570. Chapter 11: throne. Other translations use the word “chair” for this Greek term , but George Zervos argues that the Temple was the actual location of the original annunciation here (“An Early Non-Canonical Annunciation Story,” Society of Biblical Literature 1997 Seminar Papers, Vol. 36, pp. 677-679). Cf. also Michael Peppard, The World’s Oldest Church: Bible, Art, and Ritual at Dura-Europos, Syria (Yale), 2016, pp. 155ff; Gos. Bart. 2.15ff. Chapter 16: the water of the Lord’s rebuke. A tradition stemming from Numbers 5:11-31. Cf. Nutzman, op. cit., pp. 559-563. Chapters 18 through 21: The earliest Greek manuscript, the Bodmer Papyrus V (dating to the late third or early fourth century), contains a much more abbreviated version of these chapters (cf. the Appendix above). Michel Testuz, Papyrus Bodmer V: Nativité de Marie (Bibliotheca Bodmeriana),1958, pp. 102-113; Thomas A. Wayment, The Text of the New Testament Apocrypha (100 – 400 CE) (Bloomsbury T&T Clark), 2013, pp. 68-70, 273-276. Cf. also George Themelis Zervos, “Christmas with Salome,” in Amy-Jill Levine and Maria Mayo Robbins, eds., A Feminist Companion to Mariology (T&T Clark), 2005, pp. 77-98. Chapter 19: unless I examine her condition. This reading in the longer version is well attested by several manuscripts. De Strycker selects another reading: unless I insert my finger and examine her condition. Some manuscripts read unless I see. Others use the word hand instead of finger. Cf. Émile de Strycker, La Forme la plus ancienne du Protévangile de Jacques (Société des Bollandistes), 1961, p. 158; Bart D. Ehrman and Zlatko Pleše, The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Tranlsations (Oxford University Press), 2011, p. 62; and George T. Zervos’ edited article, “Caught in the Act: Mary and the Adulteress,” pp. 26ff, on-line at http://people.uncw.edu/zervosg/Pr236/New%20236/Caught%20in%20the%20Act%20Final%20-%20Edited.pdf . Cf. p. 28, where Zervos writes that “the overwhelming witness of the [manuscript] tradition of the [Infancy Gospel of James] confirms … the ‘explicit Johannine parallel’ [i.e., John 20:25] … cannot be considered with any degree of certainty to be the original reading.” Chapter 20: Salome examined her. This reading in the longer version is from the same manuscripts used for the reading in Chapter 19 noted above. Other readings include Salome inserted her finger into her nature / condition, she inserted her hand into her, Salome examined her nature / condition, and she observed her. Cf. de Strycker, op. cit., p. 160; Ehrman and Pleše, op. cit., p. 62. In personal correspondence dated October 11, 2018, Dr. Samuel Zinner comments on the word examined ( sēmeiōsōmai ) used here: “According to LSJ, sēmeioō can in a medical context mean primarily note down , take notice of . However, secondarily it can mean diagnose , and later examine , as in Paul of Aegina Pragmateia Book 6 ch. 96 (7th cent. CE), where a physician uses fingers to examine for fractured ribs.” Chapter 23: your life. Literally, “your blood.” Chapter 24: his avenger. Cf. 2 Chron. 24:20-22.

t: Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book XVIII, chapter 5
x: Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book XVIII, chapter 5 The chapter is reproduced whole. Section 1 reports the destruction of Antipas's army by Aretas and the popular reading of it as revenge for John; section 2 is the account of John, his baptism, his influence and his execution; sections 3-4 turn to the Herodian family and to Vitellius. Whiston's bracketed numerals are his own footnote markers and are left where he printed them. William Whiston translation (1737), via Christian Classics Ethereal Library. Public domain. Original page . HEROD THE TETRARCH MAKES WAR WITH ARETAS, THE KING OF ARABIA, AND IS BEATEN BY HIM AS ALSO CONCERNING THE DEATH OF JOHN THE BAPTIST. HOW VITELLIUS WENT UP TO JERUSALEM; TOGETHER WITH SOME ACCOUNT OF AGRIPPA AND OF THE POSTERITY OF HEROD THE GREAT. ABOUT this time Aretas (the king of Arabia Petres) and Herod had a quarrel on the account following: Herod the tetrarch had, married the daughter of Aretas, and had lived with her a great while; but when he was once at Rome, he lodged with Herod, (15) who was his brother indeed, but not by the same mother; for this Herod was the son of the high priest Sireoh's daughter. However, he fell in love with Herodias, this last Herod's wife, who was the daughter of Aristobulus their brother, and the sister of Agrippa the Great. This man ventured to talk to her about a marriage between them; which address, when she admitted, an agreement was made for her to change her habitation, and come to him as soon as he should return from Rome: one article of this marriage also was this, that he should divorce Aretas's daughter. So Antipus, when he had made this agreement, sailed to Rome; but when he had done there the business he went about, and was returned again, his wife having discovered the agreement he had made with Herodias, and having learned it before he had notice of her knowledge of the whole design, she desired him to send her to Macherus, which is a place in the borders of the dominions of Aretas and Herod, without informing him of any of her intentions. Accordingly Herod sent her thither, as thinking his wife had not perceived any thing; now she had sent a good while before to Macherus, which was subject to her father and so all things necessary for her journey were made ready for her by the general of Aretas's army; and by that means she soon came into Arabia, under the conduct of the several generals, who carried her from one to another successively; and she soon came to her father, and told him of Herod's intentions. So Aretas made this the first occasion of his enmity between him and Herod, who had also some quarrel with him about their limits at the country of Gamalitis. So they raised armies on both sides, and prepared for war, and sent their generals to fight instead of themselves; and when they had joined battle, all Herod's army was destroyed by the treachery of some fugitives, who, though they were of the tetrarchy of Philip, joined with Aretas's army.. So Herod wrote about these affairs to Tiberius, who being very angry at the attempt made by Aretas, wrote to Vitellius to make war upon him, and either to take him alive, and bring him to him in bonds, or to kill him, and send him his head. This was the charge that Tiberius gave to the president of Syria. Now some of the Jews thought that the destruction of Herod's army came from God, and that very justly, as a punishment of what he did against John, that was called the Baptist: for Herod slew him, who was a good man, and commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, both as to righteousness towards one another, and piety towards God, and so to come to baptism; for that the washing [with water] would be acceptable to him, if they made use of it, not in order to the putting away [or the remission] of some sins [only], but for the purification of the body; supposing still that the soul was thoroughly purified beforehand by righteousness. Now when [many] others came in crowds about him, for they were very greatly moved [or pleased] by hearing his words, Herod, who feared lest the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion, (for they seemed ready to do any thing he should advise,) thought it best, by putting him to death, to prevent any mischief he might cause, and not bring himself into difficulties, by sparing a man who might make him repent of it when it would be too late. Accordingly he was sent a prisoner, out of Herod's suspicious temper, to Macherus, the castle I before mentioned, and was there put to death. Now the Jews had an opinion that the destruction of this army was sent as a punishment upon Herod, and a mark of God's displeasure to him. So Vitellius prepared to make war with Aretas, having with him two legions of armed men; he also took with him all those of light armature, and of the horsemen which belonged to them, and were drawn out of those kingdoms which were under the Romans, and made haste for Petra, and came to Ptolemais. But as he was marching very busily, and leading his army through Judea, the principal men met him, and desired that he would not thus march through their land; for that the laws of their country would not permit them to overlook those images which were brought into it, of which there were a great many in their ensigns; so he was persuaded by what they said, and changed that resolution of his which he had before taken in this matter. Whereupon he ordered the army to march along the great plain, while he himself, with Herod the tetrarch and his friends, went up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifice to God, an ancient festival of the Jews being then just approaching; and when he had been there, and been honorably entertained by the multitude of the Jews, he made a stay there for three days, within which time he deprived Jonathan of the high priesthood, and gave it to his brother Theophilus. But when on the fourth day letters came to him, which informed him of the death of Tiberius, he obliged the multitude to take an oath of fidelity to Caius; he also recalled his army, and made them every one go home, and take their winter quarters there, since, upon the devolution of the empire upon Caius, he had not the like authority of making this war which he had before. It was also reported, that when Aretas heard of the coming of Vitellius to fight him, he said, upon his consulting the diviners, that it was impossible that this army of Vitellius's could enter Petra; for that one of the rulers would die, either he that gave orders for the war, or he that was marching at the other's desire, in order to be subservient to his will, or else he against whom this army is prepared. So Vitellius truly retired to Antioch; but Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, went up to Rome, a year before the death of Tiberius, in order to treat of some affairs with the emperor, if he might be permitted so to do. I have now a mind to describe Herod and his family, how it fared with them, partly because it is suitable to this history to speak of that matter, and partly because this thing is a demonstration of the interposition of Providence, how a multitude of children is of no advantage, no more than any other strength that mankind set their hearts upon, besides those acts of piety which are done towards God; for it happened, that, within the revolution of a hundred years, the posterity of Herod, which were a great many in number, were, excepting a few, utterly destroyed. (16) One may well apply this for the instruction of mankind, and learn thence how unhappy they were: it will also show us the history of Agrippa, who, as he was a person most worthy of admiration, so was he from a private man, beyond all the expectation of those that knew him, advanced to great power and authority. I have said something of them formerly, but I shall now also speak accurately about them. Herod the Great had two daughters by Mariamne, the [grand] daughter of Hyrcanus; the one was Salampsio, who was married to Phasaelus, her first cousin, who was himself the son of Phasaelus, Herod's brother, her father making the match; the other was Cypros, who was herself married also to her first cousin Antipater, the son of Salome, Herod's sister. Phasaelus had five children by Salampsio; Antipater, Herod, and Alexander, and two daughters, Alexandra and Cypros; which last Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, married; and Timius of Cyprus married Alexandra; he was a man of note, but had by her no children. Agrippa had by Cypros two sons and three daughters, which daughters were named Bernice, Mariarune, and Drusius; but the names of the sons were Agrippa and Drusus, of which Drusus died before he came to the years of puberty; but their father, Agrippa, was brought up with his other brethren, Herod and Aristobulus, for these were also the sons of the son of Herod the Great by Bernice; but Bernice was the daughter of Costobarus and of Salome, who was Herod's sister. Aristobulus left these infants when he was slain by his father, together with his brother Alexander, as we have already related. But when they were arrived at years of puberty, this Herod, the brother of Agrippa, married Mariamne, the daughter of Olympias, who was the daughter of Herod the king, and of Joseph, the son of Joseph, who was brother to Herod the king, and had by her a son, Aristobulus; but Aristobulus, the third brother of Agrippa, married Jotape, the daughter of Sampsigeramus, king of Emesa; they had a daughter who was deaf, whose name also was Jotape; and these hitherto were the children of the male line. But Herodias, their sister, was married to Herod [Philip], the son of Herod the Great, who was born of Mariamne, the daughter of Simon the high priest, who had a daughter, Salome; after whose birth Herodias took upon her to confound the laws of our country, and divorced herself from her husband while he was alive, and was married to Herod [Antipas], her husband's brother by the father's side, he was tetrarch of Galilee; but her daughter Salome was married to Philip, the son of Herod, and tetrarch of Trachonitis; and as he died childless, Aristobulus, the son of Herod, the brother of Agrippa, married her; they had three sons, Herod, Agrippa, and Aristobulus; and this was the posterity of Phasaelus and Salampsio. But the daughter of Antipater by Cypros was Cypros, whom Alexas Selcias, the son of Alexas, married; they had a daughter, Cypros; but Herod and Alexander, who, as we told you, were the brothers of Antipater, died childless. As to Alexander, the son of Herod the king, who was slain by his father, he had two sons, Alexander and Tigranes, by the daughter of Archelaus, king of Cappadocia. Tigranes, who was king of Armenia, was accused at Rome, and died childless; Alexander had ason of the same name with his brother Tigranes, and was sent to take possession of the kingdom of Armenia by Nero; he had a son, Alexander, who married Jotape, (17) the daughter of Antiochus, the king of Commagena; Vespasian made him king of an island in Cilicia. But these descendants of Alexander, soon after their birth, deserted the Jewish religion, and went over to that of the Greeks. But for the rest of the daughters of Herod the king, it happened that they died childless. And as these descendants of Herod, whom we have enumerated, were in being at the same time that Agrippa the Great took the kingdom, and I have now given an account of them, it now remains that I relate the several hard fortunes which befell Agrippa, and how he got clear of them, and was advanced to the greatest height of dignity and power.

t: Origen, Against Celsus, Book I, chapter 47
x: Origen, Against Celsus, Book I, chapter 47 Origen answers Celsus by pointing to Josephus: the Baptist's existence and his rite are reported by a writer who did not believe in Jesus, and who lived soon enough after the events to be a witness rather than a legend. Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 4 (1885), via New Advent. Public domain. Original page . I would like to say to Celsus, who represents the Jew as accepting somehow John as a Baptist, who baptized Jesus, that the existence of John the Baptist, baptizing for the remission of sins, is related by one who lived no great length of time after John and Jesus. For in the 18th book of his Antiquities of the Jews, Josephus bears witness to John as having been a Baptist, and as promising purification to those who underwent the rite. Now this writer, although not believing in Jesus as the Christ, in seeking after the cause of the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple, whereas he ought to have said that the conspiracy against Jesus was the cause of these calamities befalling the people, since they put to death Christ, who was a prophet, says nevertheless — being, although against his will, not far from the truth— that these disasters happened to the Jews as a punishment for the death of James the Just, who was a brother of Jesus (called Christ), — the Jews having put him to death, although he was a man most distinguished for his justice. Paul, a genuine disciple of Jesus, says that he regarded this James as a brother of the Lord, not so much on account of their relationship by blood, or of their being brought up together, as because of his virtue and doctrine. If, then, he says that it was on account of James that the desolation of Jerusalem was made to overtake the Jews, how should it not be more in accordance with reason to say that it happened on account (of the death) of Jesus Christ, of whose divinity so many Churches are witnesses, composed of those who have been convened from a flood of sins, and who have joined themselves to the Creator, and who refer all their actions to His good pleasure.

t: Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas): the baptism site
x: Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas): the baptism site Al-Maghtas, on the east bank of the Jordan in Jordan, is the principal traditional location of Jesus's baptism by John. It has been excavated as an archaeological site, not merely venerated as one. What the excavations found Roman and Byzantine remains: churches, monastic cells, pilgrim installations, water channels and baptismal pools, with occupation and building phases from roughly the Roman period through the Byzantine and into the Islamic era. The inscribed and structural evidence points to continuous Christian commemoration across centuries — the site was built up because people came to it, again and again, for a very long time. UNESCO inscribed it in 2015 as "Bethany Beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas)" for exactly that reason: the remains testify to a durable tradition of pilgrimage and baptism, not to a single datable event. What it establishes, and what it does not It establishes that the east-bank Jordan location was commemorated as the baptism site from at latest the fourth century, with substantial infrastructure built for the purpose. It does not identify the precise stretch of river where John stood. The Jordan's course has shifted, later buildings are superimposed on earlier ones, and pilgrimage geography tends to consolidate around one convenient site rather than preserve a fixed point in a meandering river. The Fourth Gospel also names Aenon near Salim as a place where John was baptizing (John 3:23), and its location is disputed. Any map of John's activity should distinguish places the texts name from places the later tradition confidently identified. Read more UNESCO World Heritage List, Baptism Site "Bethany Beyond the Jordan" (Al-Maghtas) . John 3 in this archive, for the Aenon reference.

t: The Sozopol relics: what the AMS and DNA study actually reported
x: The Sozopol relics: what the AMS and DNA study actually reported In 2010, excavation near the church of Saint John the Forerunner on Sveti Ivan island, off Sozopol in Bulgaria, produced a reliquary containing human and animal bones and a small inscribed box naming Saint John and his feast day. The published study Kostova and colleagues published the scientific analysis in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports (29, 2020). Two results matter: Radiocarbon. One human metacarpal gave a calibrated date of 5-75 CE at 68.2% probability. That range is compatible with the lifetime of John the Baptist. Ancient DNA. The samples yielded very little human DNA, and none of the damage patterns expected of genuinely ancient molecules. The authors concluded that the sequences obtained most likely came from modern contamination. What it establishes, and what it does not It establishes that a relic tradition attached to John existed at that church, that the bones are old enough not to be disqualified by their date, and that no usable genetic profile was recovered. It does not identify the individual. Age compatibility is the weakest possible form of identification: a date range covering the first century fits millions of people. The same logic would "confirm" almost any first-century bone. Reports that DNA had "proved" the relics belonged to John inverted the study's own conclusion, which was that the DNA evidence was uninformative and probably contamination. Read more Kostova et al., AMS dating and ancient DNA analysis of bone relics associated with St John the Baptist , JAS: Reports 29 (2020), 102082.

t: The "cave of John the Baptist" near Suba
x: The "cave of John the Baptist" near Suba In 2004 the archaeologist Shimon Gibson published a cave on Kibbutz Tzuba, west of Jerusalem, proposing it as a place John used. The identification is the most contested item in this collection. What is in the cave A rock-cut installation with a plastered basin and channels, a carved standing figure holding a staff, and Iron Age and later pottery. Gibson's reading is that the basin and channels served a purification ritual, that the figure is a schematic holy man, and that Byzantine-era inscriptions and pilgrimage use show later veneration of the spot. Why the identification is disputed James F. Strange's review, in Biblical Archaeology Review , accepted the interest of the ritual installation while rejecting the chain of inference: an uninscribed figure cannot be identified as John, plastered basins of this kind are not unique, and later veneration would demonstrate only that later communities believed something about the cave — not what happened in it in the first century. The gaps between "ritual installation", "figure", "John" and "this cave" are each filled by argument, not by finds. The monograph remains useful as a report on the installation. It is not evidence that John lived in, taught in, or baptized anyone in that cave. Read more James F. Strange, review of The Cave of John the Baptist , Biblical Archaeology Review , 2011.

t: Machaerus: the fortress on the ridge
x: Machaerus: the fortress on the ridge Machaerus is a Herodian palace-fortress on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan. Josephus places John's imprisonment and execution there, and the site is the one location in the story that archaeology can actually inspect. What the site contains Herodian masonry, a fortified wall circuit, a palace wing, cisterns, a bath house and a courtyard large enough for a royal gathering. Excavation has run in campaigns since the 1970s, with the most recent work directed by Győző Vörös under the American Center of Research in Amman. The architectural sequence — Hasmonean, Herodian, later Roman — is published in excavation reports rather than inferred from the literary text. What it establishes, and what it does not It establishes that the setting of the Gospel and Josephan narrative existed as a real Herodian stronghold, furnished and defensible, in the right period and the right region. It does not identify a prison cell, a banquet hall where a dance took place, or a burial place. Those are readings of the texts laid over the stones; a room big enough for a royal party preserves no record of what was said in it. The frequent labels — "Salome's dancing floor", "John's cell" — are interpretive, and the excavation reports do not authorize them. Josephus adds a detail the Gospels do not: after Antipas's army was destroyed by Aretas, popular opinion read the defeat as divine retribution for the execution of John. That is a statement about how the death was remembered, not a record of the execution itself. Read more ACOR, Excavations at the fortified royal palace of Machaerus , Győző Vörös research overview, 2016. Josephus, Antiquities XVIII.5 in this archive: the chapter that names the fortress.

t: John and Qumran: a comparison, not an affiliation
x: John and Qumran: a comparison, not an affiliation The Essene-and-Qumran hypothesis is the most durable attempt to give John a setting. Wilderness, ritual purity, moral severity, scriptural interpretation and expectation of divine intervention all appear both in the Gospels' John and in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The question is what that overlap proves. The argument for a connection John is placed in the Judean wilderness, baptizes in the Jordan, calls for repentance and moral reform, and announces that God is about to act. The Qumran community withdrew to the desert, practised repeated ritual washing, demanded purity and studied prophecy. Isaiah 40:3 — "prepare the way of the Lord" — is quoted in the Gospels of John's ministry and appears at Qumran. A family of priests in the Judean hill country (Luke 1) fits the community's priestly profile. Why the argument does not close Similarity inside one religious culture is expected, not diagnostic. No scroll names John, and none identifies him with the Teacher of Righteousness. The community's washing is repeated and sectarian; John's baptism is a single public act with an eschatological frame. Jeffrey P. García's reassessment disputes the assumed geographical proximity and the claim that both used Isaiah 40:3 in the same way, and Adinolfi and Taylor argue that the parallels are broad Second Temple patterns rather than a line of affiliation. The most defensible statement: John belongs to the same religious world as the Qumran community, and may have encountered its ideas. A childhood at Qumran, or an expulsion from it, is a modern reconstruction with no direct evidence. Read more Jeffrey P. García, “A Voice Cries Out”: Reassessing John the Baptist's Wilderness Relationship to Qumran , Journal of the Jesus Movement in Its Jewish Setting 9 (2022).

t: Christian worship, art and liturgy
x: Christian worship, art and liturgy John's Christian afterlife is the largest of any figure in this archive except Jesus. It is not evidence about the first century; it is evidence about what communities did with him, and it is unusually well documented in institutions that can be checked. The calendar Two feasts carry him: the Nativity of John the Baptist on 24 June (Luke 1 supplies the date six months before Christmas), and the Beheading on 29 August. The Byzantine and Latin calendars, the Orthodox synaxaria and the Roman martyrology all transmit them, and the 24 June feast is old enough that Augustine preaches on its relation to the solstice. The images John is one of the most painted figures in Christian art, in three recurring types: the forerunner who points at Christ (the Deesis ), the ascetic in camel hair with a reed cross, and the severed head on a platter. The Met's painted copy of the Deesis mosaic from Hagia Sophia, Leonardo's Saint John the Baptist in the Louvre, and Caravaggio's Beheading in Valletta's St John's Co-Cathedral are all documented works in documented collections — useful precisely because the provenance, not the legend, is what can be verified. The liturgical texts The Orthodox synaxis and the Latin solemnity present John as the greatest of those born of women and as the forerunner, drawing on Matthew 11:11 and Luke 1:76. The texts are institutional statements about how the churches read him; they are not independent historical testimony, but they show the shape the figure took in worship. Read more Orthodox Church in America, Synaxis of the Holy Glorious Prophet, Forerunner and Baptist John . Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch, the same synaxis . t: The Mandaeans
x: The Mandaeans The Mandaeans are the only surviving religious community that treats John — in their own language, Yuhana — as a central figure on his own terms rather than as a forerunner to Jesus. They are also the hardest case in this archive to use as historical evidence, because the community's literature is late, its language is eastern Aramaic, and its relationship to first-century discipleship is precisely what is in dispute. Who they are An ethno-religious community historically of southern Iraq and Khuzestan in southwestern Iran, with a substantial diaspora since the 2003 war. Their scriptures include the Ginza Rabba (the Great Treasure), the Book of John ( Drasha d-Yahya ), and liturgical and magical texts. John appears as a priest and teacher within a cosmogony of light and darkness, saviours and the ascent of the soul. He is not the founder of the religion in its own account, and describing Mandaeans as Christians who preferred John misrepresents a separate religion. What their practice shows Baptism is central and repeated: the maṣbuta , performed in flowing water called yardna — Jordan — with priestly actions around the immersion. That a living community has baptized in running water in John's name for centuries is real evidence of a durable tradition. It is not evidence of an unbroken institutional line back to the Jordan Valley. Why the lineage question stays open Rudolf Macuch, Jorunn Jacobsen Buckley and Şinasi Gündüz have defended versions of a Palestinian origin and eastward migration; other scholars stress the Mesopotamian character of the language and the community, and the difficulty of documenting any link to John's own disciples. Edmondo Lupieri's account is useful precisely because it separates the attraction of an origin story from the evidence needed to establish it. The Book of John's own portrayals of John, Jesus and Miriai are better evidence for the encounters of a later community with Jewish, Christian and Islamic traditions than for the first century. Read more Kurt Rudolph, Mandaeans ii. The Mandaean Religion , Encyclopaedia Iranica , 2008. Edmondo Lupieri, Mandaeans i. History , Encyclopaedia Iranica , 2008. Charles G. Häberl, The Mandaean Death of John , Alpha 1 (2017). James F. McGrath, Polemic, Redaction, and History in the Mandaean Book of John , ARAM Periodical 23 (2013). t: Yahya in Islam
x: Yahya in Islam In the Qur'an, John is Yahya, son of Zakariyya: a prophet in his own right, promised to an aged father, honoured as chaste and righteous, and given wisdom in childhood. Four surahs carry the material, and they are the primary record of the Islamic John. What the Qur'an says 3:38-41 — Zakariyya's prayer in the sanctuary, the announcement of a son named Yahya, "a word from God", noble, chaste, a prophet among the righteous. 6:85 — Yahya grouped with Zakariyya, Jesus and Elias among the righteous. 19:2-15 — the extended annunciation scene; Yahya given judgement as a child, compassion, purity, devotion, and peace on the day he is born, dies and is raised. 21:89-90 — Zakariyya's prayer answered; the family hastening in good works. The Qur'an does not narrate John baptizing Jesus, and it does not carry the Gospel story of the dance, the platter and the execution. Calling him "John the Baptist" in English imports a role the Qur'anic text does not give him. Surah 19's emphases — birth, righteousness, peace at death — are the Islamic account's own priorities. What later tradition adds Ḥadīth material integrates him into Islamic teaching: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3207 places Yahya and Jesus together in the second heaven during the night journey, and Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2863 attributes five injunctions to him — worship without partners, prayer, fasting, charity, remembrance of God. These are later religious witnesses to his authority, not contemporary records of his sermons. The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus contains a shrine associated with Yahya, on the site of a church of John. The building and the tradition are demonstrable; the identity of the relic is a separate question. Read more Qur'an 3:38-41 , 6:85 , 19:2-15 , 21:89-90 — text and translations.
